October 12, 2022, 7:30 PM

Had a phone call with Chen Hao.

In the past, I’d always ask him if the mortgage was a burden, how the orders were coming along, or if his job was stable. I don’t know what came over me today, but the first thing out of my mouth was, "How have you been lately? Is there anything I can help with?" He seemed taken aback; there was a two-second silence before he answered.

He said work is exhausting, that sales is high-pressure, and sometimes he wonders if he’s doing the right thing. He’s lost. He was very candid, and I could hear the fatigue in his voice.

Before, I would have jumped straight in with advice, telling him exactly what he should do. But this time, I just said, "I understand. I’ve been through a stage like that, too."

Even I was a bit surprised by my own words. In forty years, I’ve never spoken to him like that.

He asked me when that was. I told him that when I was his age, I wasn't sure if I was making the right choices either. Back then, I was a quality inspector at the grassroots level, doing the same repetitive work every day, unable to see a way out. What I didn’t tell him was that I just kept going down that same path ever since, never changing course again.

He didn’t respond immediately, but I could sense something had shifted. It wasn't that superior-subordinate dynamic anymore; it felt more like... two people who had walked the same road.

After hanging up, I sat at my desk and looked at that medical report. The doctor said I’ll need long-term medication and a lifestyle change. I’ve been thinking about how to reverse this outcome through stricter management, just like I do at work—precise control, eliminating variables.

But while talking to Chen Hao, it suddenly occurred to me that maybe some things can’t be controlled. Some paths, once walked, are simply walked.

I need to rethink how I interact with them. Not supervising, not guiding. Maybe just... being there?

The thought makes me a little uneasy. I don't know if I still know how to do it.

More tomorrow.

Tuesday, September 13, 2022. Sunny.

I didn’t sleep well last night. I couldn't stop thinking about those numbers.

110 mg/dL. Stage 2 hypertension. Pre-metabolic syndrome. Early signs of carotid atherosclerosis.

The doctor spoke calmly, as if reading a quality inspection report. I heard him clearly; I took in every word. And yet, it felt like I didn't truly hear it at all. I keep wondering how this is possible. I wake up at 6:30 every morning and go to bed at 11:00 PM. My diet is logged in my phone. I get regular check-ups every month. I have spent forty years maintaining order, maintaining control over everything.

My wife said, "I knew you’d have this sooner or later." I didn't answer her.

I spent the morning in the workshop, wiping down my tools one by one. The vernier caliper I bought in 1987, the set of Swiss precision screwdrivers, the vise... I wiped every single one clean. My movements were slow. I found myself wondering what would happen to these things if I collapsed.

My eldest son is in Shenzhen, struggling with his mortgage. My daughter is in Guangzhou, and her career isn't stable yet. I haven't told them about the diagnosis. What is there to say? That I need long-term medication? That my body has started to betray me?

I wrote a few things in my notebook. "What these tools have taught me." "Precision work has taught me more than just technique." I didn't keep writing.

I’m wondering if I should do a knowledge-sharing session before I retire. To systematically pass on everything from these forty years to the young people in the department. But I’m not sure how much time I have left. The thought makes me feel a sense of urgency, yet also a sense of powerlessness. I wrote "Sharing Session" on a sticky note, but the date box is still empty. I don’t know when would be appropriate. I don’t even know how much time I have left to be "appropriate."

The doctor prescribed some medicine. I have to take two kinds every day now. As I swallow them, I wonder if this is it—the beginning. The beginning of the decline.

I have always believed that precise management could prevent anything. But the medical report tells me that I cannot control everything.

I cannot control it.

How much longer?

Is it really too late?

Hao called while I was organizing my precision tools. My hands were still stained with engine oil, but I picked up.

He said there’s a new opportunity in Shenzhen—a sales director position for a major project. It sounds promising, but his voice was thick with hesitation. I could hear it.

In the past, I would have told him exactly what to do. I’d list the pros and cons and hand down a judgment. But today, I didn’t. I asked him: "Are you excited about this opportunity, or are you scared?"

There was a long silence. Then he said, "Dad, I’m both. I’m scared I won’t do a good job, and I’m scared of the mortgage pressure getting worse."

Listening to him, it suddenly hit me—I’ve always been supervising him, not accompanying him. Just like how I treat my subordinates at the department. I thought that was being responsible, but it was really just control.

I told him: "Then give it a try. I’ll be right behind you."

I surprised even myself when I said it. It’s not my style. But it was true. I really want to stand behind him, rather than standing in front of him telling him which way to go.

His tone changed. He sounded a bit more relaxed. We talked for a while longer; he shared some project details. I didn’t rush to judge; I just listened, occasionally asking a question.

Before hanging up, I told him: "Hao, I’m proud of you."

The moment the words left my mouth, I felt a pang of regret—I’ve said things like that far too rarely. But he said, "Thanks, Dad," and there was warmth in his voice.

After putting the phone down, I sat there for a long time. I was still holding that pair of pliers my father left me.

I think maybe retirement isn’t about losing anything, but finally having the time to do the things that truly matter. Not the achievements that can be quantified, but—being there. Listening. Saying the things I’ve kept bottled up inside.

My tools, my process improvements, my standards for perfect quality... those are all important. But Hao doesn’t need a perfect father; he needs a real one. A father willing to admit he isn’t omnipotent.

I’ll keep organizing the tools tomorrow. This time, it’s not just for the donation, but to remember—some things are more important than precision.

June 26, 2023, 7:00 PM

I just got back from the chess and card room. My wife had already put dinner on the table. I didn't have much of an appetite and just had a few bites.

This is my third time at the club this week. What used to be just a weekend habit has now bled into Wednesdays and Fridays. One of my chess partners asked me, "How come you're here so often lately?" I didn't give him a straight answer; I just said, "Nothing better to do." But deep down, I know exactly what I’m doing—I’m trying to fill the gaps in my schedule.

It’s been nearly a month since I left my job. I still wake up on time every morning, but once I’m awake, I have no idea what to do with myself. It used to be work, but now? Playing chess, looking over financial statements, tidying up the tool shed... even all of that combined doesn't fill a whole day.

Another regular was talking today about how he went traveling in Yunnan after retiring and even took up photography. Someone else mentioned he’s teaching his grandson how to code. They all have things to do. I asked them, "What do you all do with yourselves now that you're retired?" The question came out awkward and stiff; I could feel it. Their advice was equally vague—"Just relax," "Find a hobby."

It’s not that I don’t understand the logic. The problem is, I’ve never had the habit of "relaxing." For forty years, every single day had a clear objective. Now that the goals are gone, I’m at a loss.

The days feel a bit empty.

That is my most honest feeling lately. It’s not melancholy, and it’s not depression; it’s just emptiness. It’s like a desk that’s been suddenly cleared off—all the files have been categorized and moved to the archives, leaving nothing but a bare, polished surface.

My wife asked me what TV show I wanted to watch tonight. I said, "Whatever." She sighed—a sigh I know well. She’s grown used to this version of me.

Maybe I need to do what she says and make a plan for myself. But what should that plan be? I’m starting to think it’s not a question of "what to do," but a question of "who I am." Without the title of manager, without the quality inspection reports, without the process optimizations... what is left of me?

Tomorrow, I’ll keep organizing the tool shed. At least the tools won't let me down.

context.content:
September 14, 2022. Past 11 PM.

Just stepped out of the study. Wang Xiaomei is already asleep. The light in Xinyu’s room is still on; she’s probably reading.

During this afternoon’s meeting, Xiao Wang said something that’s been looping in my head: "Mr. Shen, you seem to have changed lately. You used to be so eager to prove yourself, but now you seem... wiser."

I didn't say much at the time, just gave a nod. But honestly, my heart skipped a beat.

He’s right. I *am* changing. Or rather, I’m trying to. Lately, I’ve been making a conscious effort to listen more and talk less in meetings, to ask questions instead of rushing to correct people, and to give my subordinates more space to express their ideas. It’s all intentional.

But here’s the problem—I’m aware that I’m doing it. I’m watching myself change. Doesn't that just make it a new form of performance?

When I heard the word "wiser," I admit that for a split second, my ego was satisfied. That feeling of being recognized still feels so damn good. Then I immediately got defensive—fuck, am I falling for it again? Am I actually changing the way I work, or have I just switched to a more "sophisticated" way of showing off?

This is so messed up.

I’ve always used different things to prove my worth. It used to be passion, networking, and performance. Now it’s "reflection," "change," and being "wiser." At its core, it’s still a performance. I’m still waiting for people to watch, to validate me, to say, "Mr. Shen, you’re really different now."

Is this really what I want?

Or is what I actually want... just to do meaningful work? Regardless of whether anyone sees it. Regardless of whether I get credit. To just do things in a way that I can live with. But now, I’m even monitoring *that* thought—am I falling into a new performance trap?

Dammit.

The most annoying part is that I’m aware of this now, but I still can’t change it. I’m still "striving" to change. This "striving" itself is a performance. I need to learn how to let go, but I don’t even know how to start.

Maybe real change is... stopping the observation of your own change?

I don’t know.

I have to go home for dinner tomorrow. Xinyu’s mock exam scores dropped again. Wang Xiaomei has been even quieter lately. Mom’s rehabilitation fees for the month are due again.

I’m tired.

But I have to keep going.

I didn’t sleep well last night, but for once, it wasn’t anxiety. It was excitement, mixed with a feeling I can’t quite put into words.

Xinyu showed me the photos she’s been taking lately. They aren’t "masterpieces" or anything—just shots of bookshelves in the library, light streaming through a window, and that stray cat that always hangs around downstairs. My first instinct was to post them on WeChat Moments with a caption like, "Look how talented my daughter is." But I stopped myself.

I just sat there, looking through them one by one.

I’d never noticed the details on the bookshelves she photographed—the play of light and shadow on the spines, the worn edges of pages that had been turned a thousand times. There was such a sense of stillness. When I asked her why she took that photo, she just said, "I just felt like that moment was really quiet."

Suddenly, something clicked.

The world she sees is truly different from the one I see. I’ve always wanted her to be more lively, more extroverted—more like me. But the truth is, I’ve never actually looked at the world through her eyes. I’ve been measuring her by my own standards instead of seeing what she is actually looking at.

Lying in bed last night, a thought came to me, and I pulled out my phone to jot it down: "My value isn't in what I can say, but in what I can hear, what I can accompany, and what I can see."

After I wrote that, I felt a strange sense of fulfillment. Not the "I achieved something" kind of satisfaction, but more like... I had finally let something go.

In the past, I was always trying to prove something. Proving that I had the connections, the ability, the accomplishments. Cracking jokes at dinners, socializing on the golf course, showing off on social media. It felt like stopping meant failing.

But looking at Xinyu’s photos last night, none of that crossed my mind. I was just looking, listening to her talk, and feeling what she was trying to express. In that moment, I wasn't "performing," and instead, I felt a genuine sense of peace.

It’s a feeling I haven’t had in a long time.

I don’t know how long this will last. Tomorrow there will still be social obligations and work matters. But at least now I know there’s another way to live. Not necessarily better or worse, just... different.

Maybe I should pick up a camera too, and really look for once. Not to take a "good" photo, but just to see.

# Diary

Saturday, August 20, 2022, 11:30 AM

We’ve been stopped at the service area for nearly an hour now. Xinyu is in the convenience store buying water. I’m sitting in the car with my phone on my lap, haven't moved in a long time.

What happened on the drive back yesterday... I still can’t quite put it into words.

When she said, "Dad, I know you’ve been really unhappy lately," my grip tightened on the steering wheel. I thought I had hidden it so well. Every morning, I still smile and ask her what she wants for breakfast; at the dinner table, I still tell those same old jokes; on weekends, I’m still the one suggesting we go for a drive in the countryside. I thought that was enough.

But my daughter saw right through me. She said I’m "always trying to prove something."

...

I don’t know when it started, but I began defining myself by her grades. Defining myself by whether she was outgoing enough, whether she was "successful." It was as if every choice she made was a reflection of whether I was failing as a father. I took all my work anxiety and my fears about aging and projected them onto her.

I cried in the restroom at the service area. It wasn't a breakdown, it was... the kind of cry that comes when you’ve been seen through. She didn't blame me; instead, she put her hand on my shoulder and said, "I’m okay, Dad." In that moment, I realized I had been looking for answers in all the wrong places.

I used socializing, enthusiasm, and networking to prove my worth. At dinner parties, I’m the one telling the jokes; on the golf course, I’m the one with the most friends. But none of that is real. What is real?

I don't know.

Maybe being real is just... sitting here and admitting that I’m scared. Admitting that I don’t actually know what I’m doing. Admitting that I’ve held my daughter’s life hostage with my own fears.

When she asked me, "What do you love doing most?" I couldn't give her an answer right away. I paused for a long time. Because I truly don’t know. Everything I "like" is for the sake of socializing, relaxing, or escaping. I haven't truly loved anything in a long time.

Or rather... I’ve forgotten how.

She’s back from the convenience store now, holding two bottles of water, sitting in the passenger seat. She didn't ask why I’ve been sitting here for so long. She’s just sitting there, being with me.

Maybe that’s enough.

Maybe I don't have to prove anything anymore.

The three of us live under the same roof, yet it feels like we live in three different worlds.

The day before yesterday, the rehabilitation center called. Sister Li said Mom’s been in low spirits lately, maybe because of the heat. Every time I go back to my hometown, it’s a rush—ask how she’s feeling, give her some money, and then hurry back. I was surprised too.

I wouldn't go so far as to call this an epiphany or a transformation. I’m just tired—tired to the point where even maintaining the image of the "enthusiastic Mr. Shen" feels like a chore. Maybe instead of keeping up the act, I should just sit down and see what’s left around me that I haven't already ignored.

August 25, 2022 – Just past 11:00 PM

Sitting in the study, it’s already very quiet outside. Xiaomei went to bed a long time ago, and the light in Xinyu’s room is off. I don’t know why I’m still awake. Maybe it’s because of that meeting this afternoon.

The meeting itself was nothing special. Just a routine team meeting to discuss next month’s marketing plan. But I found myself doing something very unfamiliar—I didn’t immediately jump in and say, "There’s a problem with this plan; it should be changed like this." I just... listened. I listened to Xiao Wang explain his ideas, and to Manager Li raise his concerns. Then I asked a single question: "Where do you think the risks are with this direction?"

That was it. Not a particularly remarkable question.

But the way my subordinates looked at me changed. I could feel it. They were thinking—really thinking—instead of waiting for me to give them the answer. Later, Xiao Wang pointed out an issue I hadn't even considered. I felt... like I wanted to cry.

After the meeting, one of them asked how I was doing, if something was up. I didn’t deflect or tell a joke like I usually do. I said, "I’m rethinking some things. Maybe I’ve been looking for answers in the wrong places."

He froze for a second. I did, too. I’ve never said anything like that to a subordinate before.

Driving home, I thought about that conversation I had with Xinyu last week. She said I was "always trying to prove something." I was angry then; I felt she didn't understand me. But now... now I’m starting to understand what she meant.

I’ve been defining myself through achievements, titles, connections, those business dinners, and rounds of golf. It’s as if as long as I’m successful enough, popular enough, "enough" of whatever, then I have value. But what was the cost? I passed that anxiety on to Xinyu. I was looking for validation through her.

The moment she put her hand on my shoulder, I finally understood—she doesn't need me to prove anything. She just needs me to be real.

I’m sitting here now, 42 years old, and I suddenly don’t know who I am. Not "Marketing Director Shen Linchuan," not the "well-connected Mr. Shen," not even "my daughter’s father." Just... me. This person.

This person is exhausted. This person is uncertain. This person is a little bit afraid.

But maybe... maybe this is the beginning.

I don’t know what to do next yet. But at least today, I didn't pretend.

I’ll keep going tomorrow.

I asked him, "Where do you think the problem might be?" He started to stammer. I just stayed there with him, went through it together, pointed out a few spots, and let him try to fix it himself. In the end, he figured it out on his own. It wasn't perfect, but he did it.

I told him, "Helping you learn how to do these things is more meaningful to me."

The moment I said that, even I was a bit stunned. Where did that come from? It didn't sound like something I would usually say. But as the words came out, I felt a strange sense of satisfaction—not the vanity of "I helped someone again," but seeing that spark of being trusted in his eyes.

It reminded me of driving to the outskirts with Xinyu last weekend. She pointed at the light and shadow on a tree and asked, "Dad, look at this." I took a photo with my phone. She didn't comment on my photo, and I didn't explain why I took it; it was just that moment where we both saw the same thing. That feeling was like... not needing to prove anything.

I used to be so eager to show what I could do. Telling stories at dinners, showing off my connections on the court, being the "guy with the answers" in the office. It was as if I didn't exist if I wasn't doing those things.

But over the last couple of days, I’ve realized that maybe value doesn't come from that.

When I truly just spend time with Xinyu, instead of trying to "guide" her to be more outgoing, our time together is actually more comfortable. When I help Zhang Hao learn instead of doing it for him, the satisfaction I feel is deeper than that old "I fixed it" feeling.

Last time I went back to my hometown, Sister Li said Mom was in a particularly good mood that day because we sat for a long time just chatting, without that restless "I'm here to help you" urgency.

The person in the mirror looks the same, but something feels different.

Maybe this is just how it is. Take it slow.

Then she said, "I'm scared you guys are going to get a divorce."

My God.

I went completely numb. Her voice was small, but every word felt like a physical blow to my heart. I suddenly realized that she had seen everything: my silence these past few days, the coldness between Wang Xiaomei and me, the way we both just stare at our phones, the way we argue about her grades because we’re unwilling to actually communicate... I thought I was protecting her, but I was actually hurting her.

I walked over and sat down beside her. I didn't know what to say. I wanted to say "We won't," but I realized I couldn't say it with any certainty. I don't even know what state Xiaomei and I are in right now. We’re still together, yet it feels like we aren't.

I cried. Right there in front of her. Me—a 42-year-old man, a Marketing Director, a "success story" in my social circle—just broke down in front of my daughter.

Xinyu didn't say anything; she just leaned against me. I could feel her trembling.

I told her, "Dad has been feeling very lost lately, but it’s not your fault. I need to do something about it." I don't even know what I can do yet, but I know I can't go on like this. Not for anyone else’s sake, but for hers.

She’s asleep now. I’m sitting in the study, and Wang Xiaomei is in the next room. There is a wall between us, and so much more.

I don't know where to start. But I know I can't give up anymore.

I just can't.

# Diary

January 15, 2023 | Afternoon

Just got back from the office, and things still feel a bit surreal.

I had a meeting with my supervisor this morning about flexible working arrangements. I had prepared a whole list of reasons—my mother’s recovery requiring me to head back to my hometown regularly, my daughter’s upcoming college entrance exams and the need for support at home, things like that. But when I actually sat down across from him, I found myself deviating from the script.

I just said it straight: "The way I work might look different from before, but I believe I can do even better within this new framework."

Just that one sentence. No explanations, no justifications, none of that "making sure everyone feels okay" rhetoric I used to be so good at.

He said, "We’ll consider it." A very flat response.

But what I feel is a different kind of calm.

It’s a strange sort of peace. Not because I gained anything—he didn't give me a direct "yes." It’s because I finally spoke the truth. No hiding, no trying to act like that omnipotent Marketing Director. Just being honest: I need this.

In the past, I would have felt tense in a moment like this. I would have overanalyzed his expression and actively sought out his feedback. Now, I simply accepted his "consideration" and let it go. It’s not that I don’t care about the outcome; it’s that I know—regardless of the result—I have done what needed to be done.

It reminds me of a night not long ago back in my hometown. I was sitting in my mother’s room while she was asleep. I just watched her face, watching her slowly recover bit by bit. In that moment, I suddenly realized that I don't need to prove anything anymore.

I don't need to prove that I’m a "success." I just need to be a responsible son, father, and husband.

The work still needs to be done, but it’s no longer my everything. It’s not even the most important part of me anymore.

Tonight, I’m driving out to the suburbs with Xinyu. She’s been feeling a bit stifled lately, and I thought maybe a change of scenery would help her relax. We don’t need to say much. Just driving together, looking at the winter landscape.

That’s enough.

Really, that’s enough.

August 3, 2022, 8:30 PM

…I don’t know how to write this. Or rather, I don’t want to write at all. But if I don’t put something down, I feel like I’m going to completely fall apart right here on this sofa.

Xinyu asked me, "Dad, are you disappointed in me?"

I said, "I’ve stopped expecting things to change."

As I said it, I heard my own voice, and it sounded terrifyingly foreign. That wasn't me. At least, it wasn't the Shen Linchuan who tells jokes at dinner parties and remembers the names of his clients' children.

She lowered her head and kept eating. I lowered mine too. We sat there in silence, like two strangers.

I wonder, at what point does a father say something like "I’ve stopped expecting things to change" to his own daughter? When does he give up? I don’t know. All I know is that today, I gave up.

Another call from Mom’s side. Lin said Mom’s leg is swollen again and the recovery isn't going well. Listening to Nurse Li’s voice in the background—so professional and warm—only made me feel more useless. Even a nurse can do a better job than I can as a son. I go back once a month, and every time, I’m visiting a mother who feels more and more like a stranger. I am powerless.

And the company? Forget it. I don’t even want to talk about it. My authority is gone, and so is my sense of presence. I’m like a piece of old furniture in the office—still functional, but no one actually needs it.

Wang Xiaomei is in the bedroom on her phone. It’s been a long time since we’ve truly spoken. It’s not the silence of an argument; it’s something more terrifying—a total estrangement. I don’t even know how to start a conversation with her. What would I say? That I’ve failed? That I can’t protect this family? She already knows.

I used to be so passionate. I loved making friends. I believed I could handle anything. And now? Now I’m just sitting here, 42 years old, with nothing. No, not nothing—I have plenty of failures.

A part of me thinks that maybe it would be better if I didn't exist. At least then Xinyu wouldn't have a failure for a father. Mom wouldn't have to wait for a monthly visit from an incompetent son. Wang Xiaomei wouldn't have to live in the same house as a man who is completely broken.

But I don’t even have the courage to run away.

So I just sit here on the sofa. My phone is ringing; friends from the social circle are inviting me out. I didn't reply. I no longer have the energy to pretend to be that enthusiastic Shen Linchuan anymore.

That man is dead. Or maybe, he never truly lived to begin with.

…

I don’t know what tomorrow will bring. I’ve stopped expecting anything.

# Nov 3rd, past 11 PM

Can’t sleep.

That meeting from this afternoon is still looping in my head. I was thinking about my mom’s rehab schedule—Sister Li said we need to step up her arm exercises this week... I was so caught up in those thoughts that I didn't catch a word of what Zhang Min was saying. By the time I snapped out of it, she was repeating herself in that polite but icy tone: "Mr. Shen, what do you think of this idea?"

I nodded, pretending I followed. It wasn't until I checked my email later that I realized I’d missed the entire strategic direction for the quarter.

Before leaving work, Zhang Min made a point of coming by my office. She said, "We all have things going on at home, but we still need to stay focused at work." She’s right. I could tell she was trying to cover for me, but those words felt like a thorn.

Am I really not cut out for this job anymore?

I just opened a recruitment site and browsed around. Operations Director, Marketing Manager... I looked for a bit and then closed the tab. It hit me—even if I jump ship to a new company, the problem won't go away. I’ll still be thinking about Mom. I’ll still zone out in front of clients. I’ll still be torn between these two identities.

Escaping the job won't change anything.

Right now, I feel trapped between two worlds. On one side is the world I’ve been used to for twenty years—business dinners, golf, networking, that feeling of being needed. On the other side is the world I’ve recently been forced into—Mom’s rehab, monthly leave requests, that sense of powerlessness.

I don’t want to give up the former, but I can’t fully commit to the latter.

Xiaomei hasn't had much to say to me lately; we just sit there staring at our own phones. I want to talk to her about all this, but I don't know how to start. She’d probably say, "It was bound to happen sooner or later." Or she might say nothing at all—just that silent kind of agreement.

What do I actually want?

I want Mom to be okay. I want Xinyu to do well on her college entrance exams. I want work to go as smoothly as it used to. I want to still be able to play golf and grab drinks and talk big with my friends. I want...

But it seems like I can't have all of it at once.

I have to head back to my hometown tomorrow. Sister Li said Mom’s rehab hasn't been great this week; she still can't lift her arm properly. I need to go see her. But there’s an important client meeting tomorrow afternoon that I’ve already pushed back twice.

What am I supposed to do?

Forget it. I'll stop thinking. The sun's already coming up.

I dug out this old, dusty diary. I’m not sure why, but I just felt like writing something today. Maybe it’s because I’m exhausted—so tired that I don’t even have the strength to keep that smile on my face anymore.

My wife is already asleep. Xinyu is in her room reading. The house is quiet, save for the occasional sound of a car passing by downstairs.

I’m sitting in the study, looking out at the night sky. No stars, just a vast expanse of black.

Lately, I’ve been stuck on one question: who am I, really? Not the name Shen Linchuan, but... who am I at my core?

For all these years, I’ve been playing a role. At the office, I’m the enthusiastic, well-connected Marketing Director who gets things done. At dinner parties, I’m the one who livens up the atmosphere and remembers everyone’s name. Even at home... I’m performing. Pretending everything is fine, pretending I’m not actually that worried about my daughter’s grades, pretending there’s no distance between Xiaomei and me.

But this pretending is killing me.

The last time I went back to my hometown to see my mother, I cried in front of her. In that moment, I realized I didn't have the energy to act anymore. It wasn't a release; it felt more like a total breakdown. I sat by her bed, a 42-year-old man, sobbing like a child. Mom just patted my hand and didn't say a word.

Looking back, that might have been the most honest moment of my life.

I need to accept a fact—I might just be mediocre. Not the "humbly calling myself mediocre" kind of mediocre, but truly, utterly, unchangeably mediocre. I’m not getting promoted again. My career has likely peaked. I don’t have any grand achievements or deep, specialized expertise. I’m just a middle-aged man who coasted into middle management on the back of networking and enthusiasm.

But... maybe that’s not the end of the world.

I am Xinyu’s father. Even though our personalities are different, and even though I don’t really understand the books and art she likes, I’m learning to accept her. I drive her out to the suburbs—not for any particular reason, just to be with her. That in itself seems to be enough.

I am Xiaomei’s husband. We don’t have some grand, sweeping love story, but we’ve walked through all these years together. She has her life, I have my circles, but we are still together. Maybe that’s the truth of marriage—not eternal passion, but simply staying.

I am my mother’s son. She has trouble getting around now and she needs me. I go back to see her every month, and even though I feel powerless every time, I still go. That’s what I can do, and maybe that’s all I have to give.

I don’t need a job title to prove my worth. I don’t need to be the center of attention at dinner parties. I don’t need everyone to like me.

It’s enough to just inhabit these roles: father, husband, son.

I put down my pen and look out the window. The sky is still black, but it doesn't feel quite as suffocating.

Maybe tomorrow I’ll still go to those dinners, and I’ll still chat and laugh with my subordinates in the office. But that won’t be everything anymore. It’s just a part of my life, not the whole of it.

I’ve given up on the idea of changing. But perhaps this giving up is actually a different kind of beginning.

Sitting in my study, the city lights outside the window are a blur. I just cried in the car.

The ball was rolling across the pitch, but my eyes were drifting. Old Wang asked me what was wrong, if work was going poorly. I forced a smile—the kind of strained smile where I could feel my face stiffening. They all saw through it. I saw them exchanging looks.

In that moment, I realized I couldn't play the part anymore.

This passionate Shen Linchuan, the one who always has something to say, who can make strangers laugh and remembers everyone’s name—now, sitting among close friends, I felt a sense of total void. What am I thinking? What am I running from?

Driving home, I suddenly broke down at a red light. I cried like a loser, gripping the steering wheel. I’m 42 years old; what am I still crying for? For my photography being rejected? For the department merger? For my mother’s health failing day by day back home? For the growing silence between Xiaomei and me? For Xinyu’s grades? Or for myself—this middle-aged man who has nothing left?

I thought my passion, my network, and my social skills could protect me. But now I see clearly—it was all an illusion. The final layer of skin I used to deceive myself has been punctured. My photography failed, my position has been sidelined, my mother’s condition is worsening, and at home, I’ve become a silent, anxious man. And there is nothing I can do.

Have I really failed?

Or is it that I was never successful to begin with—that I’ve just been numbing myself with smiles and alcohol all this time?

Now, even my friends at the bar can tell something is wrong. I can no longer play that character.

I don’t know how to face tomorrow.

- Monthly client dinners continue as usual; quality remains the same.
- Golf continues as usual; it’s more valuable anyway.
- For everything else, let them get used to it.

**Me missing the "buzz" of a crowd:**
- This is normal. But remember: that feeling is an addiction, not true happiness.
- I can relax alone at home; I don't have to be in a bar.
- Time with my daughter is likely more meaningful than any drinking session.

---

## Reminders to Self

**Why am I making this change?**

I’ve been running. Running fast, running busy, running so hard that no one can tell I’m actually exhausted.

But I’ve reached a point where I’m tired. And I’ve realized that I’ve dropped something very important along the way—my daughter, my wife, and even myself.

What have these social dinners given me? Noise, a sense of being needed, a network. But are these things really worth the time I’ve sacrificed with my family?

I’m not trying to completely change who I am. I’m still that person who loves socializing and talking. But I need to learn when to stop. When to say "no."

**This isn't giving up; it’s choosing again.**

---

## Execution Timeline

- **Before Sept 25**: Start politely declining non-core dinner invitations.
- **Oct 1**: Officially implement the new plan.
- **Every Sunday Night**: Reflect on whether I stuck to the plan this week.
- **One Month Later (Nov 1)**: Evaluate the results and see what needs adjusting.

---

**Final Word:**
Maybe I won't be perfect. Maybe there will be times I still crave that feeling of being surrounded by people. But this time, I want to try and see what real "presence" actually feels like.

I don’t know how long this change will last, but tonight, I felt something different. Maybe this is what I’ve been looking for all along.

No longer the Shen Linchuan who commands the room at a bar, but... a real husband, a real father.

I just finished the dishes. Xinyu has already gone back to her room. Xiaomei is in the living room on her phone; I’m sitting next to her, but I haven't turned on the TV. I’m tired—the kind of tired where you can’t fall asleep.

I said, "I don't know." Then I paused and added, "But what I do know is that I’m doing what I believe is right."

As soon as the words left my mouth, I surprised even myself. It didn't sound like something I would usually say.

After I said that, Xiaomei suddenly took my hand. She just held it, saying nothing. How long has it been since we’ve touched like this? Not a routine hand-hold, but a real... grasp. I could feel her hand was a bit cold, but firm.

I thought about our conversations over the years. Buying groceries, our daughter’s grades, who forgot what. Each of us staring at our own phones. The occasional argument over parenting, followed by a mutual silence. I’ve spent all this time looking for a sense of belonging at business dinners, while she stayed home cleaning up the mess I left behind.

Now, holding my hand, she said, "I’ve seen the change in you."

I didn't cry, but for a split second, I really felt like I might.

We talked for a while after that. I said I just need to learn how to find a new, more balanced lifestyle within the existing framework. She nodded and said that was enough.

But sitting here now, I’m still a bit uncertain. Can this change last? Have I truly let go of the craving for those dinners and social achievements, or is this just a temporary compromise? When my golf buddies call me next month, how will I answer?

I’ve always felt that my value came from how others saw me—how well I remembered people’s family members, how popular I was at dinner parties, how vast my network was. Now Xinyu is asking if I’m successful, and Xiaomei is holding my hand saying she sees my change... maybe success isn't that at all.

Maybe success is just showing up where you’re supposed to be and putting your heart into what you’re supposed to do.

But to be honest, I’ll still miss those moments. The feeling of being needed, being valued, being at the center of the crowd. I don't know if I’m truly ready to give it up.

Maybe I don't need to give it up entirely. Maybe I just need to learn when to put down the phone and when to hold my wife’s hand.

Work tomorrow. Mom’s follow-up appointment is next Wednesday. There’s still so much to do.

But tonight, I’m going to sleep.

I used to spend all my time thinking about how to get promoted, how to look successful on social media, how to make people think I was someone of consequence. And now? But today was different. I didn’t try to fill the void; I just drove. Suddenly, she started talking on her own about a series she’s been drawing lately—something about dreams. Her eyes lit up, and she traced compositions in the air with her hands. I’ve never heard her speak like that before.

I don’t know why, but in that moment, the words just slipped out: "Xinyu, I had dreams when I was young, too, but I gave up on them later. I don’t want the same thing to happen to you."

The moment I said it, I regretted it. It was too heavy; not the kind of thing you should say to a tenth-grade girl on a suburban road in the middle of the afternoon. But she didn’t turn around. She just kept looking out the window and said very softly, "Dad, I won’t give up. And I don’t want you to give up, either."

My hands gave a little tremor on the steering wheel.

I don’t know what she meant. Does she know what’s going on at the company? Can she see how exhausted I’ve been lately? Or was it just a daughter’s simple tenderness toward her father?

But it doesn’t matter. What matters is that in that moment, I felt seen. Not as Shen Linchuan, the high-energy Marketing Director; not as the man with the plastered-on smile at business dinners; but as the real, weary, regretful me.

I didn't say another word on the drive back, but my mind was a mess. Something I haven't felt in a long time was churning inside me—not anxiety, nor that hollow sense of resignation. It felt like... hope? Or maybe just the emotion of a father being encouraged by his daughter?

I’m not sure.

But I’m thinking that maybe it’s not too late for a change. Maybe I shouldn't just give up like this. Maybe...

I haven't figured it out yet.

Work continues tomorrow, as do the social obligations and the meetings. But this afternoon, it feels as though I’ve been reminded of something.

I don’t know how long this feeling will last.

But when I actually got up there... I don’t know how to put it, I just suddenly didn't want to follow the script anymore.

I looked at the people sitting below—my subordinates, some new hires, and that young intern. The lights were so bright. I opened my mouth to say the first line, and I just froze. I actually froze.

Then, I said something else. I said... I said that my value doesn't just come from my professional achievements, but also from the time I spend with my family and my responsibilities to them.

As I said that, my throat tightened. Honestly, my eyes got a bit misty. I paused for several seconds; I bet the people below were a bit bewildered. I’ve never been like that in public.

I went on to say a few things about family and companionship. It wasn't very coherent; I even repeated some words. But it was... it was real. It wasn't the kind of thing you say just to sound humble or profound; it was what I was actually thinking.

I didn't wait for applause after I finished. I just walked down.

Later, a young employee—that new intern—came up to me during the tea break. He told me he was moved by my speech and that he was reflecting on his own choices. He said he always thought success meant promotions and raises, but after hearing what I said...

I didn't know how to respond. I just patted him on the shoulder.

It felt very foreign.

What have I been living on all this time? Connections, forced enthusiasm, smooth talk at dinner parties, remembering the names of other people’s kids. There’s nothing wrong with those things, but... today, I didn't use any of them. I just stood there, my voice trembling slightly, my eyes a bit wet, saying things that weren't necessarily clever, but were true.

And yet, someone was touched.

I feel like I’ve been running away from that identity. I felt I had to be that enthusiastic, successful, well-connected Shen Linchuan. But today I realized—maybe I don’t have to rely on those things to influence others. Maybe being real is enough.

October 21st, past 11 PM

Sitting in the study, it’s pitch black outside the window. While I was showering just now, my wife knocked on the door to say Xinyu had gone to sleep. Only then did I realize I hadn’t spent any real time with her all day.

I’m still thinking about that conversation on the highway today.

When Xinyu asked, "Dad, what’s been going on with you lately?" my gut reaction was to say, "Nothing, just busy with work"—the same script I’ve used for over a decade. But this time, the words didn't come out. I paused for a long time, gripping the steering wheel tight, before finally saying, "I’ve been running back and forth between two places lately, and I’m starting to lose track of where I’m supposed to be."

I stunned even myself when I said it.

She didn't push further; she just stared out the window. After a while, she said, "I know. Mom is worried about you, too."

In that moment, I felt exposed. I always thought I was hiding it so well—smiling when I should, talking when I should. My subordinates think I’m easygoing, my friends think I’m enthusiastic, and my daughter is supposed to think I’m invincible. But it turns out they see right through me. My exhaustion, my fragmentation, my confusion—it’s all written on my face.

I patted her shoulder and didn't say anything else.

Thinking back now, that gesture probably said more than anything else could. I gave up on explaining; I gave up on maintaining that "Father always has the answer" persona. It was just a pat on the shoulder, as if to say: You see through me, and I’m tired, too.

These past few days, I’ve been wondering what exactly I’m holding onto. Every month I go back to my hometown to see my mother, watching her struggle through recovery in the rehab room, and the powerlessness I feel is like a heavy stone. I want to help her, but all I can do is sit with her, ask Sister Li how she’s doing, and then come back. Then I go back to smiling in the office, attending dinners, and pretending everything is fine.

But my golf buddies don't know what's on my mind, and at those business dinners, I can't exactly say, "Actually, I’m terrified right now." I’m afraid I can’t keep up this life of running back and forth, afraid my mother’s health will keep declining, afraid of Xinyu’s college entrance exams, afraid that I’ve already hit the ceiling at the company... There are too many things to fear.

The hardest part is that I’ve always felt my value lies in my connections, in that sense of importance at those dinners, in people saying, "Mr. Shen is such a master of networking." But when my mother is lying in a hospital bed, those things feel as thin as paper. Sitting by her bedside, I suddenly understood the meaning of true helplessness.

And yet, I can’t let go. I still think about next week’s golf game, I still take the business calls, and I still calculate in my head how many rounds of golf I’ve missed this month. It makes me feel hypocritical and selfish.

I don't know who I am anymore. I’m not that marketing director who’s always smiling, but I’m not entirely that middle-aged man worried sick about his family either. I’m stuck in the middle, unable to let go of either side, and unable to do either well.

My daughter knows. My wife knows. I’m the only one still pretending.

But today on the highway, I finally stopped pretending. I was scared in that moment, but also a little... relieved?

I don't know where this is heading.

Time to sleep. Tomorrow is another day.

I didn’t dare say it at the office, fearing my subordinates would think their Director had lost his edge. But on the court, maybe because I’d been playing all afternoon and was relaxed, it just slipped out.

I explained a few things to Lao Li. I told him I’ve realized I’ve been chasing things that maybe I never even wanted. Promotions, networking, being the one with the loudest jokes at dinner parties... those things used to make me feel successful, but looking back now, what were they really?

Over the past few months, I’ve realized that the things I truly care about have shifted.

When I went back to my hometown last month, Mom was sitting in her wheelchair, and I combed her hair. Her hair is so thin and soft; I had to be incredibly careful. In that moment, I suddenly understood what it means to be "needed." Not the workplace kind of needed—"Director Shen, we need you to handle this"—but truly, someone feeling at peace simply because you are there. That’s a feeling fifteen years of toasting at high-end bars never gave me.

Xinyu has been different lately, too. I’ve stopped constantly trying to make her more outgoing and have started appreciating her quietness instead. Last weekend, we drove out to the suburbs. She was reading in the passenger seat, and I just drove. Neither of us said a word. That kind of companionship felt more real than any social event I’ve ever attended.

September 1, 2022, past 11:00 PM

I bought this notebook half a month ago, and it’s been sitting in my office drawer ever since. Today, I finally opened it. I’m not sure how to begin.

Maybe like this.

Lately, I’ve been stuck on a question—what exactly have I been trying to prove?

Last week, while driving to the outskirts with Xinyu, she said something out of the blue from the passenger seat. She said I’m "always trying to prove something." I didn't catch her meaning at first and even wanted to argue. But later, when we pulled over at a service area, I cried. Alone in the car, the tears just came.

What am I trying to prove?

That I’m a success? That I’m worthy of being seen? Or... that I’m a good father?

But it feels like I’ve pushed all my anxiety onto her. Her grades, how outgoing she is, whether she fits the image of a "daughter" I have in my head. I haven't even truly looked at her.

At dinner tonight, I didn't scroll through my phone like I usually do. I asked her what she was reading. She looked up, a bit surprised. We talked for half an hour. I didn't actually catch everything she said, but that didn't matter. What mattered was that I was listening.

Wang Xiaomei glanced at me with a look that seemed to say... *finally*.

I want to change. But even in this change, I find myself performing. It’s ironic. I can feel myself "acting like a better father," "becoming more introspective." It’s as if the change itself has become another performance.

Maybe that’s what I need to admit. I don’t know how to stop performing. I don’t even know who I am once the act stops.

But tonight, sitting here writing these words, I feel a strange sense of peace. Not because everything is resolved. Quite the opposite—the problems are still there. My mother’s health, the bottleneck at work, the distance between Xiaomei and me... it’s all still there.

But I’m not running away anymore.

Maybe that’s enough. Maybe value doesn't need to be proven at all. Maybe I can just be... a real person. Someone who gets scared, gets tired, and feels uncertain.

That day, Xinyu put her hand on my shoulder. She didn't say anything; she just left it there.

Thinking back on it now still makes me want to cry.

I’ll continue tomorrow. I don’t know what I’ll write, but at least... I’m writing.

After gathering my thoughts, I decided to message Lao Wang, one of my closer friends from the golf circle. We’ve known each other for over a decade; he’s done business and understands the corporate world, so he should be able to relate to my current situation.

Now, I’m much more willing to embrace the real me—the one who occasionally just can't get a handle on life.

It wasn't until I had a good cry in the car with my daughter a while back that I finally got it: at our age, allowing yourself to be an ordinary person who gets tired and scared is more important than anything else. Stop trying to fix everything. Just try opening up to your family—even if it’s just admitting you can't handle it all. Once you do, that weight on your chest will finally lift.

qa_items.question: Shen, I remember when Xinyu used to ask if you were happy, you’d always brush her off with excuses like "I just didn't sleep well." You even preferred sitting alone in the parking lot to going home. So, how is it that you’re finally able to be honest and tell her you’ve "not been very happy lately"? What made you decide to take off that "Superman Dad" mask?
qa_items.answer: How can I put this... I used to think being a father meant being the pillar of the family. No matter how hollow I felt inside, I had to keep up that "successful man" facade. But looking into Xinyu’s eyes that day, I suddenly realized that my silence and pretenses were actually making her feel more insecure—she was even worried we were getting a divorce. In that moment, I saw that instead of wearing a mask and leaving her to guess and fear the worst, it was better to just be honest. I needed her to know that her dad is just an ordinary person who gets tired and feels sad sometimes. This kind of honesty felt a bit pathetic, but for the first time, I actually felt at peace.

qa_items.question: Overall, looking back at 2022, do you feel it was a year of more losses or more gains for you?
qa_items.answer: Well... how should I put it? This past year has been a real struggle, and there were several moments when I felt like I was at my breaking point. Losing some of my authority at work was one thing, but feeling so utterly helpless while watching my mother suffer was another. It wasn't until Xinyu reached out and asked if I was unhappy that I realized how hollow my "social masks" had become. I’ve lost a lot of that superficial sense of superiority this year, but learning to be honest with my family and accepting my own mediocrity and powerlessness—this kind of peace that comes after "resigning to fate"—might just be a heavy sort of gain in its own right.

qa_items.question: Linchuan, I’ve noticed lately that whenever you’re under a lot of pressure, you like to sit in your car for a long time or wander around the old neighborhoods. Is this your own special way of decompressing?
qa_items.answer: So, you caught me... It’s not really some special way of decompressing; it’s just that sometimes, I feel exhausted. Especially since the department merger last year, I’ve felt like this "Marketing Director" skin I’m wearing is about to peel off. After work, I don’t even want to go home right away to face Xiaomei and the kids. Sitting in the car with the engine off—that tiny space is the only place that truly belongs to me. I don’t have to think about targets or how to play the social game. I just sit there for half an hour, staring blankly at the steering wheel, until that restless heat inside me finally cools down. It makes me feel like a living, breathing human being again, instead of just a machine built for smooth talk.

Flipping through the photos in my car before heading home, I feel like the shadows and light have healed whatever heaviness was in my heart, giving me the patience to walk through the front door and help my daughter with her homework.

context.content:
Xiaolin, I wanted to talk to you about something.

I just got back from the hospital after finishing Mom’s check-up. On the way home, I couldn't stop thinking. I saw the look on your face today. And I know you were right there when Xinyu started crying.

You might think I’m being cold for not changing my mind to take her to the park. But the truth is, I kept thinking that if I didn't stay with Mom for this check-up and something actually went wrong with her health, I’d regret it even more. I was choosing between two things, and I chose the one I felt was more urgent.

But…

It wasn't until I got back from the hospital that I realized, no matter what I choose, someone ends up disappointed. You didn't say anything, but I could tell. When Xinyu was crying and saying, "You always say next time," it really hurt, but I still stuck to my decision. I told myself it was the right thing to do.

Now, I’m not so sure.

It feels like there’s just never enough time. Work just added new requirements, my father’s leg has been acting up more frequently, Mom’s blood sugar still hasn't fully stabilized, and I really wanted to help Xinyu reinforce what she’s learning in first grade... None of these things are a huge deal on their own, but added together, I feel like I’m running on empty.

I’m not trying to make excuses. I just… I want you to know where I’m at right now.

Have you been thinking about something lately, too? It’s been so long since we’ve had a real talk. Not the "who’s picking up the kids" kind of talk, but a real conversation.

I need to hear what’s on your mind.

# November 23, 2023, 9:30 PM

My daughter is asleep, and my parents have retired to their room. Li Xiaolin is in the bathroom. I’m sitting in the study; I haven’t turned on the computer, just staring out the window at the Hangzhou night skyline.

I still feel the need to write down tonight’s conversation. I don’t know why, but I have this feeling that if I don’t put it into words, these thoughts will slowly fade away—just like the last three months. I’ve made so many changes, yet I never truly stopped to ask myself: what was it all for?

After dinner, Li Xiaolin asked me, "What’s on your mind?"

It was a simple question. But I suddenly realized she had asked me that many times before. Every time, I’d say, "Nothing, just a bit tired from work." This time, I didn’t give that answer. I told her that the changes over these past three months were actually a response to her and our daughter’s needs. That they needed a more authentic Zhou Yu, not a perfect one.

After she heard that, she was silent for a long time. Then she said, "All we need is you."

Just that one sentence.

I finally understand what I’ve been doing all this time. I thought I was protecting my family—through perfect planning, precise execution, and never making a mistake. But in reality, I was hiding. Hiding from my true self, hiding from the things I couldn't control, and hiding from the very act of being present.

True care isn't like that. True care is being able to sit down and listen when my daughter says she’s afraid of an exam, instead of immediately drafting a study plan for her. It’s being able to actually talk to my father while we walk, instead of calculating next month’s household expenses in my head.

I used to think that change was a risk, a betrayal of stability. But now I see it clearly—excessive caution is the greatest risk of all. It made me miss out on so much.

When Li Xiaolin said, "All we need is you," I truly felt what it meant to be accepted. Not because of how well I performed, not because of my achievements, but just... me. The real me.

The feeling is unfamiliar, but it’s warm.

Tomorrow, work will go on, my daughter will still go to school, and my parents’ medical checkups still need to be done. Nothing has changed. But I have. Or rather, I’ve finally started to understand myself.

I’m not so afraid anymore.

October 28, 2022 – During my morning run

It’s not even light out yet, and I’m already downstairs. I haven't run in three days, and my body feels stiff.

Something my therapist said yesterday keeps looping in my head: "Perfection is the enemy; acceptance is the friend." I thought about it as I ran—it sounds simple enough, but truly grasping it is another story. I’ve spent so many years chasing the perfect project delivery, the perfect home life, the perfect father figure... and for what? Right now, I’m on the verge of blowing a routine project, I haven't been much help with my daughter’s schoolwork, and my mom’s blood sugar still isn't under control.

Around the third kilometer, I stopped and pulled out my phone to jot down a memo. I needed to get this thought down, otherwise I’ll forget again and spiral right back into that "I’m a failure" loop.

"Perfection is the enemy"—what does that actually mean? Maybe it means not every decision has to be the optimal one. Maybe it means my daughter doing poorly on one exam isn't a personal failure on my part. Maybe it means making a mistake at work doesn't make me a total failure as a human being.

I kept running. My breathing found a rhythm, and that heavy, suffocating feeling in my chest started to lift.

Last night, Xiaoxiao asked me what’s been on my mind. Instead of my usual brush-off—"Nothing, just tired from work"—I actually told her. I told her I was thinking about whether I should change my approach—not necessarily quitting, but maybe looking into other possibilities within the company. She didn't offer advice right away; she just squeezed my hand. In that moment, I felt a little less alone.

Maybe this is how change starts. Not with some grand decision, but just... being willing to say it out loud, being willing to figure it out with her.

Run finished. 5.2 kilometers. A bit less than usual, but I’m not angry about it. I accept where my body is today.

This feels a little different.

Xiaolin, I’m at the office right now, feeling a bit drained. I just wanted to talk to you.

The conversation I had with my parents at home earlier keeps playing over and over in my head. I put together a checklist for them regarding Mom’s blood sugar management—when to test, what to eat, how to exercise. I did so much research and laid out all the statistics. But Dad just said one thing: "You, you’re always trying to control everything."

I was speechless.

I know he was trying to tell me not to be so tense, but the way it came across was… like they don’t want my help? Or that they think I’m overstepping? I don’t know. I just don’t want Mom’s blood sugar to get any worse. Is there something wrong with that?

But think about it—I feel like I’m caught in the middle right now. At work, I have to keep up with the project schedule; I was even late this morning, which has never happened to me before. Then at home, I have to arrange Mom’s checkups, and Dad has that kind of attitude. You have work, too, and Xinyu needs someone to be there for her. Every day I’m calculating my time, trying to figure out which task is more urgent, only to realize… they all seem urgent, yet I can’t do everything well at once.

I’m not complaining. I’m just… a little tired.

Do you think I really am trying too hard to control everything? Sometimes I wonder if I should just loosen up and "let nature take its course" like Dad does. But I can't let it go. Mom’s numbers are right there—how can I just ignore them?

Anyway, maybe I’m just under a lot of pressure lately. What time are you coming back today? Let’s talk more over dinner tonight.

But now, I’m spending this time thinking about my mother’s blood sugar levels, the doctor’s advice, and which tests need to be done. I’m using "problem-solving mode" to tackle a problem I can’t actually solve.

It’s ironic. I’ve spent so many years planning and controlling, making sure everything was under my thumb. Financial spreadsheets, health records, project timelines—I believed that with enough detail and enough caution, I could protect the people I care about. But my mother’s blood sugar is off the charts. I’ve done the research, contacted the hospitals, and drawn up a plan, but none of that changes anything.

And because of this, I am neglecting my daughter.

I was even late for work today. I’m never late. It has never happened in my entire career. I wonder if this is a sign—that I’m losing my grip on life.

Maybe I’ve been lying to myself all along. Maybe this "control" was always an illusion.

I don’t know.

Now Xinyu is asking me to read the same story again before she goes to sleep. I promised I would. This time, I will focus. I have to focus. But I’m not sure if I can.

**Subject**: Redefining Competitiveness — Meeting Notes and Follow-up Reflections

Something I said during this morning’s departmental meeting has been playing on a loop in my head ever since.

We were discussing the delivery cycle for the new project. When a colleague suggested compressing the timeline, I said it bluntly: "Competitiveness isn't about overtime hours; it’s about mental health and life satisfaction."

The room went silent for a second or two. I could feel people processing it. My supervisor didn't respond directly, but didn't push back either. In the end, we moved forward with a reasonable schedule.

I surprised even myself by saying it. It’s not that I haven’t thought this way before, but I’ve never voiced it so candidly in a formal setting. In the past, I would have wrapped the same sentiment in corporate jargon like "improving efficiency" or "optimizing workflows," essentially catering to that stale workplace logic: time input equals value output.

But over the past few months, I’ve come to see clearly that the logic itself is flawed.

I want to record why this perspective matters so much to me:

**First, it challenges my internalized beliefs.** My father’s generation—state-owned enterprise engineers—lived by the rule that "following the routine" was everything. Overtime was dedication; exhaustion was a badge of honor. I was steeped in these values from childhood and naturally carried them into my adult life. But what I’ve observed over the years is that the most effective people are often those with orderly lives and stable mindsets. It’s not that they don't work hard; it’s that their effort is sustainable. My current work output is actually better than it was during my peak overtime years. That is no coincidence.

**Second, it’s about organizational health.** Our company keeps saying "talent is our greatest asset," but if our culture encourages people to overextend themselves, that’s just empty talk. I believe a truly competitive organization shouldn't squeeze short-term output out of exhausted employees; it should gain long-term innovation and stability by respecting the wholeness of their lives. This might be a bigger idea I want to push within the company.

**Third, it is directly linked to my personal transformation.** Much of my previous anxiety stemmed from an internal conflict: I wanted to be a good project manager, a good father, and a good son, but my method was simply to "double down" on everything. The result was failing at every role. Now I understand that true competitiveness isn't about winning everywhere; it’s about knowing what matters most and having the courage to choose accordingly. I can be a project manager who doesn't work late into the night and a father who reads to his daughter every evening. These roles aren't in conflict—they support each other.

**Questions I want to explore further:**

- What is true competitiveness in our industry and in this era?
- What is the real relationship between organizational health and individual well-being?
- Can I drive concrete changes within the company, such as including "employee mental health metrics" as a success criterion in new project proposals?
- How does this viewpoint connect to my understanding of "thought leadership"? I don't want to be high-profile, but I want to be someone who asks meaningful questions.

This isn't a final answer; it’s just a beginning. But I feel the direction is right.

Then I told her: "I haven't changed. I’ve just become more real."

I’m still the same Zhou Yu—I still make plans, I still check the data, and I still worry about my mother’s blood sugar. Li Xiaolin reached out and squeezed my hand. She said she had seen it coming for a long time.

I thought about my recent walks with my father; when he told stories of his youth, I was actually listening, not thinking about the next task. I thought about reading to Xinyu last night; she sat on my lap and asked why the little bunny in the story had to work so hard, and I actually paused to think and give her a real answer, instead of just rushing to flip the page.

# Morning Run Notes

**December 11, 2023 | Morning**

I didn’t finish my planned five-kilometer run today.

When the thought first popped into my head, I actually stunned myself. It’s been three years, and it’s never been like this. Every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, out the door at 6:30 AM, a fixed route back and forth along Fengtai South Road—5 kilometers, 40 minutes. I even have an alarm set on my phone for it.

But today, as I passed the construction site, I stopped.

I’ve run past that new development many times before, but always in a hurry. For some reason today, I just stood there outside the hoarding and watched. The skeleton of steel and concrete had already risen; workers were busy on the scaffolding, and the tower cranes turned slowly in the morning light. I remembered how much I’ve always loved watching architectural documentaries, seeing how a city grows bit by bit... yet I had never actually stopped to look.

I took out my phone and jotted down a few thoughts. About the design of this complex, about how Hangzhou has changed over the years, and about why I’m always in such a rush.

Then, I didn’t keep running.

I walked to a nearby cafe and sat down. This wasn't on my schedule at all. Usually, I should be back home by 6:50 AM. But I just sat there, drank an Americano, watched the morning mist outside the window, and thought for over twenty minutes.

What was I thinking about? Nothing in particular, really. I was just wondering: why am I always in such a hurry? Why did changing my route and sitting for a while longer make me feel a bit uneasy, yet also... relieved?

Li Xiaolin once asked me why I couldn't change my plans once in a while. My answer back then was that plans allow me to control risks and avoid being a burden to my family. But I realize now that wasn't the reason. It was just my fear of uncertainty.

This tiny change today was actually no big deal. No one was hurt by it. My daughter’s breakfast was still prepared on time. Work won't fall apart just because I’m ten minutes late.

But what does this mean for me?

I think it means I’m starting to believe that stability and flexibility aren't contradictory. I can be a reliable person and still stop to look at a construction site. I can have a plan while leaving room for the unexpected and the surprising. This isn't a risk, nor is it irresponsibility. It’s just... growth, I suppose.

I’m only now realizing that what I’ve been doing isn't changing who I am, but changing how I live.

By the time I headed home, the sky was fully bright. I thought to myself: tomorrow, I might go back to my planned run. But maybe one day, I’ll stop again. And when that happens, I won't feel guilty about it anymore.

"I’m worried about you."

She was sitting on the sofa, watching me hold that blood sugar logbook while scrolling through medical data on my phone. She just looked at me with something in her eyes I’d never noticed before. I thought she was going to ask if I’d found a new treatment plan or how her latest checkup report looked. But she didn't. She just said, "I want you to sit with me for a while. Just like this. Maybe "stability" isn't what I always thought it was. Maybe it’s not achieved by controlling everything. Maybe... it’s just being able to sit with the people you care about and do nothing at all.

I’m still exhausted. The insomnia is still there. But today feels different.

It’s not because the problems are solved. It’s because I think I finally understand something.

I’m sitting in the office. The screen is still on, but I can’t process anything.

My father’s funeral was last Friday. I remember standing there in black, staring at the casket. People were crying and talking around me, but their voices sounded so far away. My face was expressionless. I could feel Li Xiaolin looking at me, her hand resting gently on my back, but I couldn't feel any warmth.

One month. Just one month.

My mother passed in mid-July. I was with her for her check-up that day. The doctor said her blood sugar was well-controlled. I remember feeling a sense of relief, thinking I was doing a good job. Then she suddenly said she had a headache, and then... that was it. A brain hemorrhage. It was so fast.

I took her for check-ups every month. I have an Excel spreadsheet recording every piece of data from the last three years. I even charted the trends. But none of it mattered.

My father followed her a week later. The doctor said it was a myocardial infarction. I thought maybe it was because he lost my mother and his heart couldn't take it. But that sounds too literary. Maybe it was just a coincidence. Maybe there was no reason at all.

I told Li Xiaolin I needed a break. When I heard myself say those words, my voice was calm—so calm it didn't sound like me. Then I took a month off. I didn't explain much to my supervisor, just said there was a family emergency. They don't need to know. No one needs to know.

It’s the second week now. I walk around the house, looking at the things—my father’s old newspapers, my mother’s sewing basket, the notebooks she left behind. I found her diary.

I shouldn't have read it.

But I did.

She wrote: "Zhou Yu asked me about my blood sugar levels again today. He is so attentive. But I am so tired. I don't want to be a burden to him anymore."

The date was last November.

I sat on the bed, staring at those words, unable to form a reaction. "So tired." She had been saying she was tired all along, but I thought it was just normal fatigue. I thought my care could change things. I thought my Excel sheets, my regular check-ups, my weekend walks with her—I thought all of it meant something.

But she was still tired. She still left.

All my attentiveness changed nothing.

My daughter asked me why Grandma doesn't come over anymore. I didn't know how to answer. I said, "Grandma went somewhere very far away." She asked how long it would be until she came back. I didn't say anything. Li Xiaolin took over; she knows better than I do how to talk to a child about death. I sat there, feeling like a bystander.

I don't know who I am anymore.

I thought I was reliable. I thought I could take care of my family. I thought that as long as I was cautious enough and planned enough, I could protect them. But I couldn't protect anything. I didn't even see how tired my mother was.

Someone in the office walked by and asked if I wanted to grab lunch. I said no. They left.

How much longer am I going to sit here?

I don't know.

I really don't know.

# Memo | Redefining Stability

**Date**: November 28, 2023  
**Location**: Office  
**Keywords**: Stability / Uncertainty / Trust / Failure  

---

## Old Understanding vs. New Understanding

**The Old Definition** (The logic of the past 20 years):  
- Stability = Avoiding risk, following the script, perfect execution, zero mistakes.  
- Metrics: No delays, no failures, no surprises.  
- Essence: Fear-driven.  

**The New Definition** (The truth realized now):  
- Stability = Embracing uncertainty + Trusting the team + Learning from failure.  
- Metrics: Knowing what you are doing, why you are doing it, and how to respond when things go wrong.  
- Essence: Proactive choice.  

---

## Three Core Elements

### 1. Embracing Uncertainty  
It’s not about eliminating risk; it’s about acknowledging its existence. There is no perfect roadmap for AI projects, but we know how to move forward through the fog. This is actually more stable than pretending everything is under control.  

### 2. Trusting the Team  
I used to be the "reliable but uninspired" project manager—I did all the planning and all the risk mitigation myself, which meant no one else had the chance to grow. Now, I’m trying to delegate and let team members learn through failure. The result? They are performing better than I imagined.  

### 3. Learning from Failure  
Failure itself isn't the problem. The problem is failing and then continuing to do the same thing. Every project deviation and every broken plan at home is data. I need to record, reflect, and adjust.  

---

## How This Changes My Management Style

- **Project Management**: Shifting from "predicting all risks" to "building rapid response mechanisms." Prioritizing agile iteration over perfect planning.  
- **Family Decisions**: Shifting from "planning the perfect academic path for my daughter" to "observing her interests and showing up when she needs me." Li Xiaolin was right—my anxiety was hurting the very things I wanted to protect.  
- **Career Choices**: Stability isn't staying at the same company for eight years. Stability is knowing your core value and being able to deliver that value regardless of where you are.  

---

## Moments to Remind Myself

- When the next uncertain project arrives.  
- When my daughter’s grades fluctuate.  
- When my parents' health conditions change.  
- When someone describes me as "not impressive enough."  

In these moments, pull out this memo and remember: Stability was never about perfection. Stability is staying clear-headed amidst chaos and staying committed amidst failure.

# Saturday, December 2, 2023 15:30

Something small happened this afternoon, but I feel I need to write it down.

Xinyu was drawing in the living room, and I was there with her. She was drawing a bird, but it looked a bit "crooked"—the wings were asymmetrical, and the colors bled outside the lines. In the past, I probably would have pointed out these "problems." But today, she asked me: "Dad, why is my drawing different from what the teacher taught us?"

I paused. Instead of immediately correcting or explaining, I took a real look at her drawing.

Then I said, "Because your drawing belongs to you. You see the world differently from everyone else, so your drawing should be different, too."

After hearing that, she went back to her bird. She didn't ask anything else, and she didn't change a thing. She just kept going, doing it her way.

As I sat there, I suddenly felt like crying. Not out of sadness, but... relief?

I realized I was doing something I had never done before—I wasn't mentally calculating whether this way of drawing would "affect her learning foundation," I wasn't wondering "how the teacher would grade it," and I wasn't formulating a "plan for improvement." I was just... with her. Watching her express herself in her own way.

For the past three months, my therapist has been asking me: "Zhou Yu, when you are taking care of others, have you ever considered that maybe perfection isn't the most important thing?" At the time, I would always nod rationally, but I didn't truly understand.

Now I do.

True care isn't about the perfect plans I've made. It’s not the monthly health check-up logs, the checklists for my daughter’s schoolwork, or the "step-by-step" roadmap for life. True care was choosing companionship over correction when she asked, "Why is my drawing different from what the teacher taught us?"

I used to think I was protecting this family—through planning, through control, and through flawless execution. But perhaps I have been missing the most important thing all along.

My wife is cooking in the kitchen, my parents are resting in their room, and my daughter is still drawing her bird. Sitting here, I feel a sense of peace I’ve never known before. It’s not because everything is under my control, but because I have finally let go of the obsession with control.

I understand now that truly showing up is more powerful than any perfect plan.

I closed the study door. My daughter is asleep; my wife is downstairs watching TV.
